title: Lake River Corp. v. Carborundum Co.
summary: A minimum-quantity damages formula was an unenforceable penalty because it required payment for unperformed services without crediting the service provider’s saved costs; ordinary breach damages remained available.
notes: The source rounds numerical examples. They illustrate the formula’s operation rather than a final damages computation. The last opinion page was checked as an image because its searchable text omits the paragraphs preserving ordinary damages and ordering remand.

sections.Parties: Lake River supplied warehousing, bagging, and distribution services. Carborundum manufactured Ferro Carbo, the abrasive powder handled under the agreement, and retained ownership of that powder until delivery to its customers.
sections.Material Facts:
At Carborundum’s insistence, Lake River installed a new $89,000 bagging system. To protect that investment and an anticipated twenty-percent profit, Lake River obtained a three-year guarantee of 22,500 tons. If the minimum was not shipped, Carborundum would owe the then-current bagging rates for the shortfall. Full performance would have generated roughly $533,000 in revenue.

Demand for domestic steel and the abrasive fell. Carborundum shipped only about 12,000 tons and paid for the work actually done. Lake River demanded roughly $241,000 for the shortfall and held approximately 500 tons of Carborundum’s finished product as leverage. Carborundum incurred extra expense serving its customers from elsewhere and challenged both the formula and the asserted lien.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the district court awarded Lake River the formula amount and Carborundum damages on its conversion counterclaim. Both appealed. The Seventh Circuit held the lien invalid and the stipulated formula a penalty, and remanded for computation of Lake River’s ordinary damages, with appropriate adjustments to the parties’ recoveries.
sections.Issue: Did the shortfall formula reasonably estimate loss under Illinois law, or did it impose a penalty by exceeding the provider’s expected compensatory recovery?
sections.Holding: The formula was a penalty. Lake River could nevertheless recover ordinary damages: the unpaid contractual revenue attributable to the shortfall, reduced by the costs saved by not performing the remaining services. The invalid clause did not invalidate the underlying bargain.
sections.Reasoning:
The formula guaranteed gross revenue while ignoring the variable costs Lake River avoided. Posner tested several breach stages. A breach immediately after purchase of the system would produce vastly more than the expected $107,000 profit, while even a breach near the end could produce an appreciable excess. This structural overcompensation, rather than a mere inaccurate forecast in one unusual event, showed that the formula did not reasonably estimate compensable loss.

Lake River’s suggestion that mitigation would reduce the stipulated sum did not cure the clause: stipulated damages are ordinarily intended to replace subsequent judicial computation. The court also distinguished real alternative performances and expressly avoided casting general doubt on take-or-pay arrangements. A label or minimum commitment alone does not answer whether a particular clause is an agreed performance or compensation triggered by breach.

Although Posner discussed arguments favoring freedom to choose penalties between sophisticated firms, the federal court was applying Illinois law in diversity. State courts, not the federal court’s preferred policy, controlled the applicable common-law rule.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Lake River makes the relationship between revenue, saved expenses, and lost profit concrete. It also illustrates how a federal court separates its policy preferences from its responsibility to apply state contract law.

topics.remedies: Preserves ordinary damages after invalidating the stipulated measure.
topics.liquidated-damages: Tests a formula across different breach stages and credits costs saved.
topics.governing-law: A federal diversity court applies state common law despite expressed policy doubts.
topics.efficient-breach: Discusses incentive and credibility arguments without turning them into the governing holding.
